newsitem.title: FRANCE: Paris says Charette snub unintentional.
newsitem.headline: Paris says Charette snub unintentional.

text.p: French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette unintentionally missed a tribute to retiring U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher at a NATO dinner and did not deliberately snub him, a senior French official said on Thursday.

"The tribute was not on the agenda and it was therefore unaware that it would take place that M. de Charette was absent from the room," the official said, commenting on an American news report that de Charette left the room during a tribute to Christopher in Brussels on Wednesday.
The official told Reuters that other prominent NATO foreign ministers were also absent. He declined to identify them.
De Charette had to leave the room to address a news conference, the official said.
Paris had earlier outright denied a report in the Washington Post newspaper that de Charette had stood up and left during a toast in honour of Christopher.
But State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns commended the article as "a very fine report".

The controversy reflected the raw state of Franco-U.S. relations, with disputes accumulating over the reform of NATO's military structure, the succession to U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, France's drive for a bigger say in the Middle East and Western policy on Zaire.

Paris had been backed in its initial denial by NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana who said in a statement released by the French foreign ministry: "After we verified with participants at the lunch, I can state quite clearly and formally there is no substance to this story."
Spokesman Burns, however, said in Washington the article, by the Washington Post's correspondent William Drozdiak, contained one inaccuracy -- the timing of the incident.
"There was only one slight factual inaccuracy in that story ... the tribute by Secretary Solana did not occur at lunch. The tribute occurred at the end of the day.
The Washington Post had reported that the purported incident occurred as Solana was proposing a toast to the secretary of state at an alliance foreign ministers' meeting in Brussels.

The Post quoted an unnamed senior U.S. official as saying: "It was an incredible display of petulant behaviour. Everybody knows there are tensions in the French-American relationship, but nobody expects them to be shown at a personal level."
De Charette called the report a "manipulation" and his spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt branded it an "ill-intentioned lie" aimed at damaging already frayed ties between Paris and Washington.
The French minister told Reuters: "I cannot explain it. But I severely condemn this kind of manoeuvring because I do not doubt this was a manipulation."

Solana said there had been no toast, since Christopher had received a farewell tribute during the earlier ministerial working session, and de Charette had not left the dining room at any moment during the lunch.

Paris and Washington frequently find themselves at odds on key global issues, but diplomats say Franco-American ties appear at a low ebb despite a warm personal relationship between Presidents Bill Clinton and Jacques Chirac.
Probably the most serious fight concerns the future of NATO's southern command, which controls the Mediterranean.

In what has been dubbed the battle for Naples, France is demanding that Washington hand over the post it has held since NATO was created in 1949 to a European. The United States has flatly refused and is not amenable to compromise. at the NATO hall."
